Christopher Love
KRIS-tuh-fur LUV
proper noun (person)
Welsh Puritan preacher (1618-1651), Presbyterian, beheaded under the Commonwealth; author of sermons on heaven, hell, and the soul.

📖 Biblical Definition

Christopher Love was a Welsh-born Puritan preacher of fervent and affecting power, a convinced Presbyterian who ministered in London during the upheavals of the English Civil War and the Commonwealth. Converted as a youth under the preaching of William Erbery, he became a bold and popular preacher, much used to awaken sinners and comfort saints. His sermons, gathered after his death into volumes such as The Penitent Pardoned and treatises on heaven and hell and the soul's immortality, press eternal realities upon the conscience with great earnestness. Love's life ended in martyrdom of a kind: a firm Presbyterian opposed to the execution of the king and to the Independent ascendancy, he was implicated in a plot to restore the monarchy and was beheaded on Tower Hill in 1651, dying with notable composure and faith, his wife's tender letters to him in prison surviving as a memorial of godly affection under the shadow of death. Love stands in the dictionary as a fervent Puritan preacher and a martyr of conscience, who proclaimed heaven and hell with burning seriousness and met his own death in the sure hope of the glory he had preached.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Welsh Puritan preacher (1618-1651), a fervent Presbyterian beheaded under the Commonwealth; a powerful preacher of heaven, hell, and the soul who met his own death with composure and faith.

CHRISTOPHER LOVE, proper noun. Welsh-born Puritan preacher (1618-1651), a convinced Presbyterian.

A bold and popular preacher in London during the Civil War and Commonwealth.

Author of sermons on heaven, hell, and the immortality of the soul.

Implicated in a plot to restore the monarchy; beheaded on Tower Hill in 1651.

Died with composure and faith, his prison correspondence a memorial of godly love.

📖 Key Scripture

Phil 1:21 — "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."

Rev 2:10 — "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

2 Cor 5:1 — "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens."

Heb 9:27 — "And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Love's preaching honors the recovery of heaven and hell as urgent realities, against a sentimental religion that has muted eternity, and his death honors the costliness of conscience against expediency.

expand to see more

Eternity-muted correction. Much modern preaching has fallen silent about heaven and hell, trading eternal realities for present therapeutic comfort. Love preached them with burning seriousness, pressing upon his hearers the weight of the soul's everlasting destiny. The dictionary holds that the certainty of death and judgment, the reality of heaven and hell, belong to the church's faithful proclamation; to mute them is to flatter sinners on the road to ruin and to rob saints of their hope.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the costliness of conscience. Love would not bend his Presbyterian convictions to the prevailing power, and it cost him his head. The dictionary commends, with sober discernment of his turbulent age, the example of a man who held his convictions under the shadow of the scaffold and met death in the hope of the glory he had preached, faithful unto death for the crown of life.
